content:
iVerify today published a report detailing P7 DarkSword, a new variant of the malware involved in the DarkSword iPhone exploit chain discovered earlier. Here are the details.

A little background

Earlier this year, Google and iVerify revealed two sophisticated iPhone hacking tools, named Coruna and DarkSword, both of which chained multiple iOS vulnerabilities to compromise devices running older versions of the operating system.

In the case of DarkSword, once an iPhone is compromised, the attacker can deploy additional malware to access sensitive data.

Coruna targets devices running iOS 13 through iOS 17.2.1, while DarkSword affects iPhones running iOS 18.4 through iOS 18.7.

The situation prompted Apple to release system updates for the affected older versions of iOS, including iOS 15.8.7, iOS 16.7.15, and iOS 18.7.7. Apple even took the unusual step of making iOS 18.7.7 available to devices capable of installing iOS 26, so that users who choose not to upgrade to the latest system version can also receive protection against DarkSword.

Google said at the time that DarkSword was being used by multiple commercial surveillance vendors as well as suspected state-backed actors, with related attacks observed in Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Malaysia, and Ukraine.

New DarkSword variant found in the wild

iVerify today announced the discovery of P7 DarkSword, an unprecedented variant found while examining an infection on an employee's iPhone at a financial institution two months ago.

In additional details provided to 9to5Mac, iVerify noted that P7 extends compatibility to iOS 18.7, one step further than the iOS 18.6 supported by the older variant they had been tracking. Other DarkSword deployments observed by Google had already supported iOS 18.7.

The company also said the threat actor behind P7 is spreading the malware via malicious advertising as part of "watering hole attacks," meaning victims are not necessarily targeted individually. Users who encounter malicious or compromised web content may fall victim as part of a broader campaign.

Below is the report content:

In August 2026, we investigated a DarkSword infection and discovered an unprecedented variant, which we have named P7 DarkSword. The name P7 comes from the p7_ variable prefix used by the threat actor when modifying the original DarkSword code. Compared to the variants we typically observe, P7 reduces its on-device footprint, adds theft capabilities targeting the device's Keychain and cryptocurrency wallets, and introduces bidirectional C2 communication with the attacker's infrastructure. This article describes the investigation, the variant's capabilities, and the indicators available for detection.

The report notes that P7 DarkSword advances beyond earlier variants in three main areas: stealth, stability, and functionality. This new variant reduces the number of processes it records and injects into, uses browser storage to avoid reinfecting the same device, and expands its data theft capabilities.

iVerify also told 9to5Mac that the changes appear to reflect substantial work by the operators rather than simple AI-assisted modifications. The company noted that P7 is better at hiding itself and cleaning up after itself, so previously known indicators of compromise (IOCs) are no longer applicable.

Most notably, iVerify said P7 can extract Keychain data directly on the iPhone before transmitting it to the attacker, rather than copying the entire Keychain database for processing elsewhere.

P7 DarkSword can also target cryptocurrency wallet data and introduces more sophisticated bidirectional communication with the attacker's command-and-control infrastructure.

This bidirectional communication also gives the attacker greater control over compromised devices. According to iVerify, P7 can receive commands to capture arbitrary files, upload photos, list installed applications, access the Apple Notes database, collect data from individual application containers, and scan the device's file system.

By default, this spyware communicates with the attacker's command-and-control server every 15 seconds to obtain new instructions, although the communication interval can be changed remotely.

It is worth noting that P7 is not a new iOS vulnerability; it is a new version of malware deployed after a successful compromise via DarkSword. iVerify did not disclose which iOS version the device was running when P7 was discovered in August.
